I have been booking travel for other people for eleven years, and I can tell you the mistake almost everybody makes. They compare the wrong thing. They open two hotels side by side and they compare the price, because the price is the number the website puts in the biggest letters. But the price is only one line of the bill. The hotel that is forty dollars cheaper is usually further from everything, and if you take two taxis a day for nine days, you have paid the difference three times over. So compare the total, not the rate. My second rule is about reviews. Do not read the best ones and do not read the worst ones. Read the ones in the middle, because those are written by people who are not angry and not in love, and they are the only ones who tell you what the place is actually like on a normal Tuesday. And my third rule is the simplest. Whatever you choose, choose the quieter one. Nobody in the history of travel has ever come home and said the room was too quiet.

Here is something people from outside the United States are often surprised by. In most American beach cities, the difference between one street and the next one is enormous. The block right on the ocean is the loudest, the most expensive and the most crowded, and it is where almost every visitor books. Walk three streets inland and the same room is thirty per cent cheaper, the street is quieter at night, and the beach is still a five-minute walk away. The trade-off is real, but it is smaller than the price difference suggests. The second thing is the shuttle. A lot of the bigger hotels run a free shuttle to the main areas, and it is almost never mentioned on the booking page, only on the hotel's own website. So before you decide that the cheaper hotel is too far, check whether it has a shuttle. Two of the three hotels I stayed in last year did, and I only found out on the second morning.
